hops.title: Compare it: a dry bean waits like a dry sponge
hops.text: Hand your child a dry kitchen sponge. It stays stiff until water swells it soft. A dry bean waits the same way, and water softens its coat. Some seeds wait far longer: UCLA scientists once sprouted a sacred lotus seed that was roughly 1,300 years old. Keep loose seeds away from children under 4 (choking risk).

sources.citation: Penn State Extension, "Seed and Seedling Biology" (updated January 14, 2025)
Stuart Wolpert, UCLA Newsroom, "Scientists sequence genome of 'sacred lotus,' which likely holds anti-aging secrets" (May 10, 2013)
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org, "Choking Prevention for Babies & Children: What Every Parent Needs to Know"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A flat dry kitchen sponge beside a plump wet sponge, with a dry bean and a soaked bean on a saucer.
image.caption: Like a dry sponge, a bean seed stays stiff until water swells it soft.

hops.title: Say it: the sprout pushes the dirt with its elbow
hops.text: "Look, it is pushing the dirt aside with its bent elbow, so its baby leaves stay tucked safe behind it." Say this the first morning you spot a bent green stem poking up. In bush beans, that bent stem takes the scrape of rough soil, then straightens out once sunlight reaches it.

sources.citation: Ha, Morrow and Algiers, Botany (Biology LibreTexts), 4.6.4: Germination
Penn State Extension, "Seed and Seedling Biology" (updated January 14, 2025)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A young green bean sprout arching up in a hook out of dark potting soil in a clay pot.
image.caption: A bush bean's bent stem pushes through the dirt first, guarding the growing tip and pulling up the seed leaves.

hops.title: Ask it: what built all those leaves?
hops.text: Ask your child, "If our bean plant did not eat the dirt, what built all those leaves?" Cheer every guess, then wave at the air and share the twist: plants build leaves mostly from water and a gas in the air, plus a pinch of soil minerals. One potted willow gained 164 pounds while its soil lost just 2 ounces.

sources.citation: S. G. Saupe, College of St. Benedict and St. John's University, "Willows and Photosynthesis: Analyzing van Helmont's Classic Experiment"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A tall leafy willow tree in a large terracotta pot still full of soil, with gentle air swirling around its leaves.
image.caption: A potted willow gained 164 pounds while its soil lost just 2 ounces. It grew mostly from water and air.
